document.title: Osama bin Laden: A Case Study (excerpt, pp. 18-22)
document.authors: Sandia National Laboratories, U.S. Department of Energy (Dr. Gary W. Richter)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), 1998 Missile Strikes on Bin Laden May Have Backfired
document.note: [Unclassified] Excerpt of pages 18-22 of the Sandia report. It finds the U.S. was not blindsided by the embassy bombings, that the East African cell was under intense scrutiny, and that the August 20 cruise missile strikes had negative political consequences, including mirroring aspects of al-Qaeda's own attacks.

persons.name: Osama bin Laden
persons.role: Leader of al-Qaeda; target of a US campaign to expose him and build a legal case after the August 1998 embassy bombings

mentions.quote: Long before bin Laden came to public attention he and his group were a well-known threat and the subject of significant attention
The attacks generated enormous publicity for bin Laden and raised him to the level of a worldwide icon for frustrated Muslim fundamentalists

organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: Described as having global reach and anti-American hatreds, making it a potential threat to all US installations overseas.

organizations.name: East African al-Qaeda cell
organizations.notes: Existence known before the bombings. Many members identified and under intense surveillance; the cell felt itself to be 'at 100% danger'.

organizations.name: U.S. State Department
organizations.notes: Its security standards and threat assessment are discussed in the embassy bombing findings.

organizations.name: Accountability Review Boards
organizations.notes: Published two analyses of the Nairobi and Dar es Salaam bombings, including the January 1999 report.

organizations.name: FBI

organizations.notes: A State Department official was recommended to be assigned there.

organizations.name: Foreign Emergency Support Team

places.name: Nairobi
places.significance: Site of the 7 August 1998 US embassy bombing. Embassy staff warned of vulnerability; the neighboring building collapsed.

places.name: Dar es Salaam
places.significance: Site of the second 7 August 1998 US embassy bombing; the bomber was stopped at the perimeter by guards and an embassy water truck.

places.name: Kenya
places.significance: Location of the Nairobi embassy bombing and most of the deaths, which were among Kenyans.

places.name: Tanzania
places.significance: Location of the Dar es Salaam embassy bombing.

places.name: East Africa
places.significance: Region of the al-Qaeda cell that was under surveillance and disruption operations.

places.name: Sudan
places.significance: The US embassy in Khartoum was closed over threat levels and Sudanese embassy personnel were moved to Nairobi.

places.name: Albania
places.significance: Cited as a place where a planned bombing of a US installation was prevented.

events.description: Truck bomb attacks on the US embassies in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam. Most deaths were innocent Kenyans in the building next to the Nairobi embassy.
State Department Accountability Review Boards published their report on the Nairobi and Dar es Salaam embassy bombings, with findings and recommendations.
Truck bomb attacks on U.S. embassies in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam; attackers failed to reach the structures, most deaths were Kenyans in a collapsed adjacent building in Nairobi.
In Nairobi the bomber failed to penetrate the outer perimeter because local guards refused to open the gates.
In Dar es Salaam the bomber was stopped by guards and blocked by an embassy water truck.
Accountability Review Boards published their report on the embassy bombings in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam.
Planned bombing of U.S. installations in Albania was prevented.

sources_cited: U.S. State Department, Report of the Accountability Review Boards on the Embassy Bombings in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam on August 7, 1998 (January 1999)
key_claims: Al-Qaeda and its East African cell were known and under surveillance before the 7 August 1998 bombings, so the US was not blindsided.
US threat assessors in Washington took the warnings less seriously than embassy staff in Nairobi did, and the threat was perhaps underestimated.
The bombings raised bin Laden to a worldwide icon for frustrated Muslim fundamentalists despite limited American casualties.
The State Department found that security standards were inadequate against large vehicle bombs and that no credible intelligence gave immediate warning.
The bombings led to an escalated campaign to expose bin Laden, build a legal case against him and destroy his network.
